chapters.name: Chapter 1: The basics of great service

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Greeting customers and first impressions
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Greet a customer warmly within seconds, in person or on the phone.
This lesson builds toward: When a customer arrives or calls, you will greet them warmly within seconds, in person or on the phone, with your name or the business name and an offer to help.
Customers decide how they feel about a business in the first few seconds. A warm greeting tells them they matter. In person, greet people quickly, even if you are busy: make eye contact, smile and say hello. If you are with someone else, a nod and "I'll be right with you" stops the next person feeling ignored.
Use a simple, friendly opener: "Hi, welcome in! How can I help today?" In a restaurant: "Good evening, welcome! Table for how many?" At an office front desk: "Good morning, who are you here to see?" On the phone, say the business name and your name: "Thanks for calling Main Street Pharmacy, this is Dana. How can I help?"
Look ready: phone away, standing or sitting up, and a clean, tidy space. Use the customer's name if they give it. Small things add up to a great first impression.
Step by step:
- Notice the customer quickly.
- Make eye contact and smile.
- Say a friendly greeting and offer help.
- Busy? Nod and say "I'll be right with you."
- On the phone: business name, your name, offer help.
Words to know:
- First impression: how someone feels about you or a business in the first few seconds.
- Greeting: the first friendly words you say to a customer.
Try it now: Write three greetings: one for a store or restaurant, one for an office front desk and one for answering the phone at a business. Say each one out loud with a smile until it sounds natural.
You can now greet customers warmly in person and on the phone.

check.q: Why does a warm greeting matter?
options: Customers judge the business in the first few seconds
It makes the line move slower
It is only needed for regular customers
check.why: First impressions shape how customers feel about the whole visit.

check.q: The phone rings while you are tidying a shelf. What would you say when you answer?
options: "Thanks for calling, this is Sam. How can I help?"
check.why: A good greeting names the business or you and offers help.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Listening to find the real need
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask questions and repeat back to understand what a customer really needs.
This lesson builds toward: Given a vague customer request, you will ask open and closed questions and repeat back the customer's real need, until the customer confirms you have it right.
Customers do not always say exactly what they need. A shopper asks for "a phone charger" but needs one that fits an older phone. A caller says "my bill is wrong" but really wants to know why it went up. Listening carefully saves time and avoids mistakes.
Let the customer finish without cutting in. Then ask open questions: "What will you be using it for?" "When did you first notice the problem?" Ask a closed question to confirm a detail: "Is that the order from Tuesday?"
Then repeat back: "So you need a charger for an iPhone 8, and you'd like it today. Is that right?" Repeating back shows you listened and catches mistakes before they happen. In a restaurant, reading the order back prevents the wrong meal reaching the table.
Step by step:
- Let the customer finish.
- Ask open questions to understand the need.
- Ask closed questions to confirm details.
- Repeat back what you heard.
- Ask: "Is that right?"
Words to know:
- Open question: a question that needs more than a yes or no answer.
- Closed question: a question answered with yes, no or a short fact.
- Repeat back: saying the customer's request back to check you understood.
Try it now: Ask a friend or family member to pretend to be a customer with a vague request ("I need something for my kitchen"). Use two open questions and one closed question, then repeat back their real need.
You can now use questions and repeating back to find out what a customer really needs.

options: A question that invites a long story
A question with a short answer, like yes, no or a date
A question you ask after closing time
A question the customer cannot answer

check.q: A customer says, "I need a gift for my dad." What would you ask first?
options: "Do you want the most expensive one?"
check.why: An open question helps you find the real need.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Solving the problem
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Take ownership of a customer's problem and offer a clear solution or next step.
This lesson builds toward: Given a customer problem you did not cause, you will take ownership and offer a clear solution, choices or the right person to help, with a next step and a time you will keep.
Customers remember how you handled their problem more than the problem itself. Own it: say "Let me help you with that," even if someone else caused it. Never say "That's not my department" and walk away.
Know what you can do. Learn your workplace's rules (policies) for returns, refunds, swaps and discounts, and who to call when something is above your level. Offer choices when you can: "I can replace it today, or refund it to your card. Which would you prefer?" If you need to pass the customer to someone else, explain why, introduce them, and tell the new person the details so the customer does not have to repeat everything.
Never promise what you cannot deliver. "I'll find out and call you by 3 pm" is better than "It'll be fine" when you are not sure. Then keep your promise.
Step by step:
- Own it: "Let me help you with that."
- Check what your policy allows.
- Offer one or two clear options.
- If it is above your level, pass it on with all the details.
- Promise only what you can deliver, with a time.
Words to know:
- Policy: the business's rules, such as for returns or refunds.
- Escalate: pass a problem to a manager or someone who can do more.
- Ownership: treating the customer's problem as yours to solve.
Try it now: Pick a common problem in a job you have or want (a wrong size, a cold meal, a missed appointment, a billing question). Write what you would say to own it, two options you could offer, and who you would pass it to if needed.
You can now take ownership of a customer's problem and offer clear options or a next step.

check.q: What does taking ownership of a problem mean?
options: Saying it is not your job
Treating the problem as yours to help solve
check.why: Ownership means you help the customer even if you did not cause the problem.

check.q: A customer needs an answer you do not know. What would you say?
options: "I'll find out and call you by 3 pm."
check.why: A clear promise with a time builds trust.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Hard moments and every channel

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Upset customers and the LAST method
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calm an upset customer using LAST: Listen, Apologize, Solve, Thank.
This lesson builds toward: With an upset customer, you will calm the customer using LAST: Listen, Apologize, Solve, Thank, using all four steps and getting help if there are threats.
Upset customers are usually upset at the situation, not at you. Staying calm is your job and your power. The LAST method gives you four simple steps.
Listen: let them speak without cutting in; nod and reflect back: "Your order came 40 minutes late and the food was cold." Apologize: say sorry for how it affected them, sincerely: "I'm really sorry, that's not the experience you should have had." You can apologize without blaming anyone. Solve: offer a fix within your policy, or bring in a manager: "I can remake it now, or take it off your bill." Thank: thank them for telling you: "Thank you for letting us know. It helps us fix it."
Keep your voice low and slow, don't argue or take it personally, and use their name. If a customer becomes threatening or abusive, you do not have to take it: get a manager or security and follow your workplace's safety rules.
Step by step:
- Listen: let them finish, then reflect back.
- Apologize sincerely for how it affected them.
- Solve: offer a fix or bring in a manager.
- Thank them for telling you.
- Threats or abuse: get a manager or security.
Words to know:
- LAST: Listen, Apologize, Solve, Thank: four steps for an upset customer.
- Sincere: honest and meant from the heart.
Try it now: Write a LAST script for one of these: a cold meal, a package that never arrived, or an overcharge. Write one sentence for each letter, then say the whole script out loud.
You can now calm an upset customer with Listen, Apologize, Solve, Thank.

check.q: What does the S in LAST mean?
check.why: LAST is Listen, Apologize, Solve and Thank.

check.q: A customer is upset that their package never arrived. What would you do first?
options: Offer a refund before they finish
Tell them it is the delivery company's fault
Listen fully and repeat back what happened
check.why: LAST starts with listening so the customer feels heard.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Phone, chat and email service
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Give clear, friendly service by phone, chat and email.
This lesson builds toward: By phone, chat or email, you will write or give a clear, friendly reply with the answer first and the next step, with every fact checked and no private details shared.
Phone: customers cannot see your face, so your voice does the work. Smile while you talk; it really changes your tone. Speak clearly, and before putting someone on hold, ask: "May I put you on a short hold while I check?" and thank them when you come back. If you must transfer, tell them who they are going to and why.
Chat: answer quickly, keep messages short, and use friendly words. Check before closing: "Is there anything else I can help with?" Email: use a clear subject line, greet them by name, answer the question in the first lines, give the next step and sign with your name. Read it once before you send it. An AI assistant can help you draft or polish a reply, but check every fact and never paste in the customer's private details.
On every channel, protect privacy. Follow your company's steps to check who you are talking to, and never ask for a full card number or password by chat or email.
Step by step:
- Phone: smile, speak clearly, ask before hold, thank them after.
- Transfers: say who and why.
- Chat: quick, short, friendly; ask "Anything else?"
- Email: clear subject, name, answer first, next step, your name.
- Protect privacy: follow ID checks, no card numbers or passwords by chat or email.
Words to know:
- Hold: pausing a call while you check something.
- Transfer: passing a call to another person or team.
- Channel: a way customers contact you: in person, phone, chat, email or social media.
Try it now: A customer emails: "I ordered a blue jacket and got a red one. What now?" Write a short reply with a subject line, greeting, apology, solution, next step and your name.
You can now serve customers well by phone, chat and email while protecting their privacy.

check.q: What should come first in the body of a customer service email?
options: A long story about your company
check.why: Customers want the answer first, then the next step.

check.q: You use an AI assistant to draft a chat reply. What would you do before sending?
options: Check every fact and remove private details
check.why: AI drafts must be checked and kept free of private details.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Following up and building loyalty
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Follow up after a problem and turn a customer into a returning one.
This lesson builds toward: After a problem is fixed, you will write a follow-up message that checks the fix and invites the customer back, sent when you promised.
A problem fixed well can make a customer more loyal than if nothing had gone wrong. Following up is how you finish the job.
If you promised a call or update, do it on time, even if the news is "still working on it". After a fix, check back when it makes sense: "I wanted to make sure the new part arrived and works." Keep simple notes in your system or notebook: name, problem, what you did, and what is next, so anyone on the team can help.
Small extras build loyalty: remembering a regular's usual order, thanking a long-time client, or telling a customer when the item they wanted is back in stock. If you run your own business, ask happy customers for a review, and treat complaints as free advice on what to fix.
Step by step:
- Keep every promise of a call or update, on time.
- Check back after a fix.
- Write simple notes: name, problem, action, next step.
- Remember regulars and thank them.
- Use complaints to improve.
Words to know:
- Follow-up: contacting a customer again to check or update them.
- Loyalty: when customers keep coming back and recommend you.
Try it now: Final task: role-play an upset customer with a friend using greeting and LAST, agree a fix, then write the follow-up message you would send the next day.
You can now follow up after a problem and build customer loyalty.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Greeting No greeting, or a cold or rushed one. A warm greeting within seconds with a name and an offer to help. Greeting fits the setting and sounds natural. Listen and Apologize Interrupted, argued or blamed. Listened fully, repeated back the problem and apologized without blaming. Named the customer's feeling and stayed calm the whole time. Solve No clear fix or next step. Owned the problem and agreed a clear fix or next step. Offered choices and gave a time for any promise. Thank Ended without thanking the customer. Thanked the customer for raising the problem. Closed by checking if anything else was needed. Follow-up message No follow-up, or it has no clear purpose. A short next-day message that checks the fix and invites them back. Personal, specific and free of errors. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why can a problem fixed well make a customer more loyal?
options: They see the business cares and keeps its promises
check.why: Handling a problem well shows the business can be trusted.

check.q: You replaced a customer's wrong order yesterday. What would you do today?
options: Send a coupon with no message
Ask them to post a review right away
Send a short message checking everything is right now
check.why: A follow-up checks the fix and shows you care.
